The Ninety-Fourth 


ANNUAL REPORT 


of the. — 


Young Men’s Christian Association 
of Montreal 


For the Year Ending March 3/st, 1945 


The Ninety-Fourth 
Annual Report 


The Board of Directors present 
herewith the 94th Annual Report in 
accordance with the requirements 
of the Constitution, It reviews a 
period which found us in the sixth 
year of global War. 

At the beginning of the period 
(April) there was a general feeling 
of intense expectancy with world- 
wide attention focused upon the 
approach of D-Day. Then came 
the exciting invasion of Norman- 
dy, followed by the heaviest kind 
of fighting, in spite of which the 
Allied Army drove across France 
to the borders of Germany itself 
freeing Belgium and part of Hol- 
land on the way. After the tem- 
Porary reverse in the Ardennes, 
our Army advanced to the Rhine 
and at the date which ends this 
report were prepared for the final 
break through into the heart of 
the enemy’s homeland and his ey- 
entual unconditional surrender. 
Throughout the year the Canad- 
ians also fought valiantly in Italy 
in the campaign which helped to 
hasten the War’s end. 


In these stirring events the Can- 
adian Navy, Army and Air Force 
took an important and effective 
part, on the sea, on land and in the 
air, In many Canadian homes, 
however, sad hearts were the price 
of victory, for our casualties were 
heavy, 


Throughout the year events on 
the “home front” were much as in 
other War years, with emphasis 
Placed on food and munitions pro- 
duction. As the crisis in the War 
was reached, serious political con- 
troversy became associated with 
the need for adequate reinforce- 
ments overseas. Inevitably this 
created divisions in the country 
endangering national unity. 


In such a setting the Montreal 
Association conducted its work, 
under limitations and stresses due 
to wartime conditions, but with 
many special opportunities and 
added responsibilities arising out 
of these same conditions. In the 
acceptance of these we have found 
our greatest satisfactions, 

In reviewing the work of the 
past twelve months it should be 
pointed out that each of our 
Branches has already had its an- 
nual meeting, and heard detailed 
reports of its own work, These 
Branches are Cestral, Westmount, 
North, Southwestern, Notre Dame 
de Grace, International and La- 
chine. Each is administered by a 
Board of Management, the mem- 
bers of ‘which are nominated by 
the members of the Branch and 
appointed by the Metropolitan 
Board of Directors. This report 
therefore will deal with matters 
of a more general interest and 
which effect the Montreal Associa- 
tion as a whole. 


Y.M.C.A. CENTENNIAL 

Undoubtedly _ the outstanding 
event of the year was the celebra- 
tion of the Centennial of the As- 
sociation, which was founded on 
June 6th. 1844, at London, England, 
by a dozen young men whose lead- 
er was George Williams. 

Montreal, where the oldest As- 
sociation in| North America was 
founded in 1851, was chosen by 
the National Council as the place 
for the official Canadian celebra- 
bration, in conjunction with the 
annual meeting of the Council held 
June 3-6, which breught together 
a large and representative group of 
Association leaders.

included:

Much of what was said on 
these occasions has been preserved 
in a Centennial Report, copy of 
which will be fyled as part of our 


permanent records, While there 
was much looking back on our 
historical achievements, there 
was more of the forward look, ex- 
pressed by our world-leader Dr. 
John R. Mott in the words, “By 
far the best days of the Y. M. C. 
A. lie in the future because of the 
larger knowledge and_ priceless 
experience that we bring to bear 
upon the tasks of the new _ cen- 
tury.” 


WAR SERVICES—SIXTH YEAR 

For the sixth year the buildings 
and equipment of the Montreal 
Association have been used by the 
men and women of the Services 
without charge. on the same basis 
as regular members. Due to the 
termination of the British Com- 
monwealth Air Training Plan 
which meant the closing down of 
many air stations, and also the 
transfer back to the United King- 
dom of the R. A. F. stations in 
Canada, as well as the acceierated 
movement of reinforcements over- 
seas, the attendance at our activ- 
ities of Service personnel showed 
a decline over previous years. 


While the attendance was reduc- 
ed there was no reduction in the 
number of activities conducted in 
all Branches in behalf ut members 
of the Armed Forces. At Central 
Branch, the use of the physical 
department by persons in uniform 
reached as high as 45 pe. ef the to- 
tal usage. In addition to a variety 
of sports activities, a very com- 
plete social program was offered 
of. dances, splash parties, after- 
noon teas and sing songs. The 
arts and crafts. library and cther 
facilities were well usd. 

The Women’s Committee which 
operated the Hospitality Corner in 
Sentral Branch lobby directed 14- 
828 to approved lodgings, provided 
laily afternoon tea, in additicn to 
many special services rendered at 
Chirstmas time and throughout the 
year, The Corner was in action 
every day of the week. 


At the Westmount Branch the 
use of the gym and swimming pool 
continued heavy throughout the 
year, The regular Saturday Night 
dances were held for 52 weeks. At 
Southwestern, North and Notre 
Dame de Grace $ranches, and to 
a iesser degree at International, 
a variety of entertainment and 
services was provided. 

A unique feature of our war 
services was the news letter sent 
out by Notre Dame de Grace and 
North Branches regularly to their 
members overseas and occasionally 
by other Branches. Numbers of 
Servicemen and women attended 
Camp Otoreke during the summer. 

Sir George Williams College 
made all their classes available to 
members of the Forces without 
charge, 448 men and women en-

At. the spring Convocation of

As the College plans its future

number of unmet _ educational 
needs in this great city. The fu- 
ture task of the College amid this 
zrowing variety of opportunities 
or service, must be studied with 
great care. Such a process of self- 


study is now underway in the 
College as it faces the challenge 
of post-war rehabilitation and re- 
construction. 


PROGRAM 


The program of the Association 
has continued to be effected by 
war conditions, as would he ex- 
pected. In spite of many difficul- 
ties however, a wide variety of 
activities have been conducted and 
every possible effort has been 
made to keep the quality high, 
and in line with the Association’s 
objectives 


(a) ADULT EDUCATION, par- 
ticularly along social and 
cultural lines has been pro- 
minent. This has included: 

(1) Arts and Crafts, included a 
great variety of interests, 
handicrafts, dramatics, pho- 
tography, woodwork, paint- 
ing and weaving. 

(2) Music Appreciation in many 
forms, listening groups, etc. 

(3 


Y 


Language Classes in English, 
French and Spanish. 
Discussion Groups, lectures 
and addresses, Citizens’ For- 
um groups. 

Public Speaking, several 

groups, including one in the 

French language. 

(6) Libraries were active, the 
College, Central and South- 
western being the three larg- 
est. 

(b) CO-EDUCATIONAL ACTIVI- 

TIES increased during the 

year, in keeping with newer 

trends. These included the 

So-Ed Program, which is a 

social-educational activity in- 

creasingly popular among 
young people; Splash and 

Dance Parties, Saturday Night 

Clubs, dances and outings.

INFORMAL GAMES were 
available in all Branches, such 
as table tennis, billiards, 
chess and checkers, and 
greatly used at “odd mo- 
ments.” Occasional compe- 
titions created additional in- 
terest. 


TEEN-AGE CLUBS have been 
active in five branches and 
tried to meet the needs of 
approximately 1,500 older boys 
and girls in high school or 
employed. These are  self- 
governing groups responsible 
to a great extent for their 
own programs. 

BOYS’ WORK received in- 
creased emphasis during the 
year, and we believe that 
progress was made. Some 
highlights of the program in- 
cluded: 

Building Activities — Five 
Branches have regular Boys’ 
Divisions with organized clubs, 
gymnasium classes, game 
tournaments, handicrafts, 
hockey groups, etc. Over 2,000 
boys were regular mem- 
bers. 


Community Boys’ Work was 
conducted in several dis- 
tricts where the Association 
has no buildings, including 
Lachine and Ville St. Pierre, 
Rosemount, Peint St. Charles, 
the East End and East 
Central districts. During the 


year a new extension work 
was organized in Peace Cen-

cance in school life. 


THREE ORGANIZED CAMPS 


were operated last summer 
under experienced leadership, 
as follows: 

Camp Otoreke for young 
people at Lake St. Joseph, 
was open for three months 
with an aggregate attend- 
ance of 1,082 camper-weeks 
and 636 week-ends. A broad- 
ening of the program to in- 
clude more educational and 
cultural features won marked 
approval of campers. Land 
and water sports, canoeing, 
Sailing, tennis—all were en- 
joyed. 

Camp Kanawana, our boys 
camp near St. Sauveur, had 
another splendid season; 400 
different boys attended for a 
total of 1,450 camper-weeks. 
A capable staff of 24 men and 
women was in charge. Sever- 
al parties of skiers used the 
camp in winter. 

Camp Perrot operated for its 
first season last summer. 


’ 


The property, located on the 
south shore of Ile Perrot, and 
consisting of about 40 acres, 
was purchased for use as a 
near-the-city camp. The lo- 
cation proved ideal for safe 
swimming, boating, games, 
hikes, etc. It was open for 8 
weeks with a total attendance 
of 300. 


COUNSELLING AND GUID- 
ANCE are among the chief 
functions of the Association 
and absorb a great deal of 
the time of our staff. Mem- 
bers and non-members, par- 
ents, employers, veterans, all 
bring matters of a personal 
nature to the secretary seek- 
ing his help. This includes 
guidance in the choice of pro- 
gram interests, in securing 
employment, in handling 
emergency situations, in deal- 
ing with family problems and 
many other matters.

CHRISTIAN EMPHASIS 


The constant testing of our 
work against the purpose and 
standards of the Association has 
been a practice for yeurs. The 
chief method is that of annual 
conferences when the program is 
appraised by the _ responsible 
groups in the light of the cur- 
rent needs of youth and our stated 
ubjectives. 


During the year the Annual 
Keymen’s Conference was attended 
by over 100 laymen responsible for 
the administration of the Associa- 
lisn, Other Conferenses included. 
the Hi-Y Regional, Junier Secre- 
taries, City-wide Staff, Hi-Y. offi- 
cers, Boys’ Work Secretaries. Re- 
gional Boys’ Work Committee men. 
Several Branches held all-day con- 
ferences for the inspiration, and 
guidance of their workers. 

The Chapel in Central building 
has continued to be a symbol of 
the spirit which we must ever strive 
to keep at the heart of the Assoc- 
iation It was used throughout 


the year for a variety of special 
services, organ recitals. induction 
ceremonies. as well as for private 
devotions. 

In all our Branches and at the 
Camp there are many opportunities 
to emphasize the Association’s 
Christian obiective. During the 
past year these have _ included, 
seasonal worship services, inspir- 
ational addresses, Lenten services, 
decision meetings, campfire talks, 
camp chapel s€rvices, tent devot- 
ions, the circulation of devotional 
literature, corporate Church attend- 
ance etc. 


COMMUNITY CO-OPERATION 


The complexity of modern  soc- 
iety and the development of num- 
orous organizations in the field of 
youth welfare make it necessary 
that the Association should develop 
co-operative relationships with 
many other private and public ag- 
encies in the community. While 
such co-operation involves a heavy 
burden of time and effort, it is jus- 
tified usually, in the interests of 
the community as a whole 

These relationships are with 
such bodies as the Montreal Ceun- 
cil of Social Agencies,, the Chur- 
ches. the Schools, the Religious 
Education Council, the War  Ser- 
vices Co-ordinating Council, the 
Montreal Christian Youth Com- 
mittee, and various government 
agencies. 

Our work also requires contacts 
with the Young Women’s Christian 
Association for purposes of clear- 
ance and co-operation, with the 
Y. M. H. A. the Youth Hostel 
Association and other youth or- 
ganizations. Our Association has 
co-operated in the work of the 
Canadian Youth Commission, in- 
cluding the Provincial Youth Con- 
ference and a local youth hearing 
held in the Association building. 
We participated in the Juvenile 
Delinquency Prevention Week. 

“Remake Clinics” have been 
conducted by the Government in 
several Branches. Various Soid- 


ier’s Wives organizations, and a 
host of social, athletic, religious 
and welfare groups have used our 


various buildings for their meet-- 


ings. In the Central building 
719 meetings of this type were 
held. The Community Garden 
League of Verdun centered in 
Southwestern Branch and _ 19,000 
cans of produce were put up in 
our canning plant, 


MEMBERSHIP 


Once again the Montreal Assoc- 
iation has reached a new “high” in 
its total number of members and 
in receipts from membership. On 
March 31st our paid membership 
was 11,748 compared with 9,841 last 
year, an increase of 1,907 persons. 
Receipts were $67,857.00 compared 
with $60,456.00 a year ago, an in- 
crease of $7401.00 While young 
men’s membership has remained 
at a low level because of enlist- 
ments in the Forces, other divis- 
ions have made up for these losses. 

Membership in the various bran- 
ches as at March 31st was as fol- 
lows:

and equipment are not included in

total number of participants dur-

be placed at 20,000 persons. 

The press, radio, printed mater-

have been used to advantage in 
keeping our work before our ~ 
members and the general public. 


RESIDENCE 


The capacity of our Stanley 
Street Residence is 547 beds, and 
during the year practically 100 
pe. occupancy has been maintain- 
ed. In addition, there is accom- 
modation for 64 men in the North 
and Westmount buildings, 


Tn all 7,245 different men were 
in residence, a decrease of 212 over 
1943-44, The total bed-nights 
numbered 200,487, compared with 
200,373 a year ago. On March 3lst, 
108 service personnel were in re- 
sidence. The gross residence re- 
venue was $157,555.76, 

During the year our accommo- 
dation was used by men of the 
Services to the extent of 49,154 
bed-nights, or an average of 135 
per night, 


FINANCE & PROPERTY 

The Annual Financial Campaign 
with an objective of $130,000. was 
held in November with a final re- 


» port of $133,596. from 4,669  sub- 


scribers. 


Walter P. Zeller was General 
Chairman and Colin W, Webster, 
Chairman of the Special Names 
Committee. H, M. Mawhinney 
acted as General Vice-Chairman, 
and §. C, Norsworthy Vice-Chair- 
man of Special Names. W. C. 
Stannard was Chairman of Pub- 
licity. A strong Teams organiza- 
tien of Division chairmen and 
workers brought the total to 600 
men and wemen who together 
made the appeal an outstanding 
success. 


The buildings and property of 
the Association continue to be 
subject to heavy wear and _ tear 
hecause of the additional usage 
by men and women of the Armed 
Forces. It has been the policy, 
however, to maintain all buildings 
and equipment as well as possible 
under the circumstances having in 
mind that certain extraordinary it- 
ems will have to be given consid- 
eration when materials and staff 
are more” readily available. In 
addition to routine maintenance 
the following major repair and 
decorating items were carried out: 
Complete decoration of the Cen- 
tral branch Lobby and_ Social 
Room by painting woodwork, walls, 
and ceiling, an operation carried 
out under the direction of the 
Building Bureau; Decoration of 
main floor corridor, Boys Depart- 
ment Game Room, Lobby and pas- 
sage to Locker Room, Billiard 
Reem. Lunch Counter, Barber 
Shop, Cafeteria Kitchen; exten- 
sive decorating in College corrid- 
ors and classrooms; replacement of 
elevator motor and sudsianiial re- 
pairs and decorating items in West- 
mount, North, Southwestern and 
International branches. 


After many years of search for 
suitable camping facilities neav the 
city for a low cost camp, the Kamp 
Kanawana Committe, was success- 
ful in lecating a property on the 
seuth side of De Perrot about 50 
miles from Montreal, which after 
careful investigation was  acquir- 
ed for $8,500. The transaction 
was completed in time for a suc- 
cessful low cost camp to be con- 
ducted during the 1944 summer 
season. 


NATIONAL COUNCIL 

As a constituent member of the 
National Council of Y.M.C.A.’s 
of Canada, the Montreal Associa- 
tion has a direct share in the work 
of the Council, which has many 
aspects, 


The chief task of the Council in 


the year under review was the sti- 
mulation of the observance of the 


Y.M.C.A. Centennal by the Associa- 
tion throughout the country. The 


special obServance in Montreal dur- 
ing the meeting ef the National 
Council June 3-6 is mentioned else 
where in this report. In addition 
many Centennial events were held 


in local Associations in all parts of 
Canada during the year and espe- 


cially in June. Special publicity ma- 
terial was prep2red, breadcasts were 
arranged, service were held and 
every possible advantage taken of 
this unique occasion to interpret 
the Association’s purpose and id- 
eals to the country at large. 

A new development during the 
year sponsored by the Council is 
the Y. M. C. A. Sports College of 
the Air, which has had a pheno- 
menal growth. This 15-minute 
radio program is broadcast through 
the co-operation of the C. B. C. 
each Saturday morning from Coast 
to Coast, reaching boys in cities, 
towns and rural communities. The 
combinaton of coaching in a var- 
iety of athletic skills, hints on 
health and fitness, and ideas on 
“claying the game” produces a 
character-building feature which 
has proved so attractive that over 
40,000 beys have enrolled, and the 
total listening audience is esti- 
m2ted at half a million. ; 


The third biennial National 
Young Peoples’ Conference was 
held at Ottawa in March, with an 
attendance fully representative of 
the Asssciation in every Province. 
The program dealt with the tran- 
sition period from war to peace. 
and the part which the Y. M. C. 
A. should play therein. 


The usual committees and de. 
partments of the Council have 
functicned he‘pfully throughout the 
year. 


Members of the staff have paid 
visits te Montreal on many occas- 
ions and their assistance has been 
greatly appreciated. 


The Study of the Canadian Y. 


M. C. A. initiated by the Council 
made good progress during the 
year. The report and its recom- 
mendations will be considered at 
a special meeting of the National 
Council to be held in October, 
1945, 


CANADIAN Y.M.C.A. 
WAR SERVICES 


During the year under review 
the Canadian Y. M. C. A. continued 
its extensive services to the men 


and women of the armed forces in 
Canada and wherever their duties 
have taken them overseas. 


In 1944 the overseas staff num- 
bered 1,072 with an additional 1,090 
volunteer workers, who operated 
with our mobile Forces at an ag- 
gregate of nearly 3000 different 
points during the year. These ex- 
tended from Iceland, through the 
United Kingdom, to the Azores, 
Gibralter, North and West Africa, 
up through Sicily, Sardina, Cor- 
sica, Elba, Malta and Italy. D- 
Day was the beginning of another 
great ‘Adventure in Service,” which 
has since carried our workers 
through France, Belgium, Holland 
and right into Germany. 


In order to keep up with and 
serve a Mobile Army—first in the 
United Kingdom and latterly in 
Italy and N. W. Europe—it has 
been necessary for the Y. M. C. A. 
to use a total of 195 motor vehic- 
les, including 3-ton lorries, lighter 
vechicl€s and mobile canteens, 

The aggregate attendance over- 
seas in 1944 at all events: enter- 
tainment, religious, educational, 
sports, personal services, tea car 
services, etc. was 31,283,524, Dur- 
ing the year 21,756 moving picture 
shows were held, while 275,254 
different sports events were con- 
ducted. Seven ice-rinks were op- 
erated by the Y.M. C. A, in the 
United Kingdom and two were 
available in N. W. Europe 

In addition to many Y. M. C. A. 
Centres conducted in barrack ar- 
eas unit and brigade lines and in 


air stations, Leave Clubs and Town 
Centres were operated as follows. 
In Italy—at Rome, Salerno, Chian- 
ciano, Florence, St. Vito and Nap- 
les N.W. Europe—Antwerp, Ghent, 
Deauville, Benny; United King- 
dom; London, four clubs; Harro- 
gate, Leeds, York, Greenock, Hor- 
sham, Leatherhead, Farnborough; 
Bordon. 

Free services included regular 
free distribution of beverages, bis- 
cuits, cigarettes, ete., in addition 
to thousands of articles of sports 
equipment, stationery, books and 
magazines. Over $20,000 was 
spent on Christmas extras, 


OUR WORLD SERVICE 

The Montreal Association has 
continued its support of the World 
Service Program of the North 
American Y. M. C. A.’s_ conducted 
through the International Com- 
mittee in 32 countries, 

During the year many of our 
overseas secretaries and _ their 
families who had been imprisoned 
were released following the re- 
capture of Manila in the Philip- 
pines. The Emergency War Ser- 
vices have continued throughout 
the Far East with the armies of 
yur Allies, including the gallant 
Shinese. One new Canadian sec- 
retary was sent out for service in 
Shina, and another for service in 
India. Encouraging new develop- 
ments have taken place in South 
America.

the financial support of the Mon- 
treal Association in 1944 by bran- 
ches:

Y.M.C.A. WAR 
FRISONERS AID 


The World’s Committee of Y. 
M. C. A.’s, with the valued help 
chiefly of Swedish and Swiss neu- 
tral secretaries and staff, has con- 
ducted 1. remarkable work during 
the past year in over 600 camps of 
prisoners-of-war in all parts of the 
world, a work conducted regard- 
less of nationality, race or creed. 

In spite of great difficulties 
supplies have been shipped regul- 
arly to the various camps, and 
periodic visits by secretaries have 
keen made to aScertain the needs of 
che prisoners. A limited amount 


of goods has been sent to the Far 


ast, although communications 

with prison camps in that area 

have been least satisfactory. 
Canadian prisoners-of-war back 


home in Canada after repatriation 
from Germany have been generous 
in their appreciation of the con- 
tributicn of the Y. M. C. A. to- 
wards the amelicration of their lot 
when “behind the barbed wire.” 
This included provision of sports 
equipment, musical instruments, 
reading matter, craft tools and 
material, motion pictures, eduea- 
tional text books, ete. 
SECRETARIAL PERSONNEL 


John W. Beaton, General Secre- 
tary has continued to act as Sen- 
ior Secretary for National Y. M. 
C. A. War Services, on loan from 
the Montreal Association. W. J. 
G. Macdiarmid, W. J. Holliday 


and A. W. Kemball have continued 
in Y. M. C, A. War Services over- 
seas. W. A. Buckley has con- 
tinued in War Services in Canada, 
Miss Freda Wales in the C. W. A. 
C. and E. F. Sheffield with the 
Canadian Navy. In September, 
W. H. Spearman returned to West- 
mount Branch after two years 
overseas as manager of the Béa- 
ver Club, London, England. 

In September Ernest I. Taylor 
was 2ppointed Executive Secretary 
of International Branch from Act- 
ing Executive Secretary at West- 
mount. 

Additions during the year  in- 
cluded: Allan D. Logan to South- 
western Branch as Program Sec- 
retary, William Kinrade to West- 
mount as Boys’ Work Secretary, 
Miss Diliys Foulkes and Roy D. 
Locke to Notre Dame de Grace as 
Women’s ‘Work Secretary and 
Boys’ Work Secretary, respectively, 
Mrs. Helen Fry to Southwestern as 
Women’s Work Secretary, Joyce 
Booth to North Branch as Instruct- 
or. 


APPRECIATION 

There are many factors which 
combine to make possible a suc- 
cessful year’s work in the Y. M. 
Cc. A. We are grateful to the 
many friends who have contrihuted 
generously of their financial re- 
sources; to the members of loards 
and Committees for their frequent 
eounsel, guidance and services; to 
the many volunteers who have 
served as friendly counsellors of 
clubs and boys in camp; coaches 
and ‘instructors; interviewers; 
teachers; ministers; to the Press; 
the members of the gymnasium and 
swimming Leaders’ Corps; the 
staff; to the Churches; the Wo- 
men’s Auxiliaries; the Montreal 
Council of Social Agencies; Rail- 
way and other corporations; the 
Young Women’s Christian Assoc- 
iation, and many other co-operat- 
ing agencies. Above all. we are in 
humility, grateful to God for His 
blessing and power. 


OBITUARIES 


We record with sorrow the pass- 
ing of a number of friends of the 
Asscciation: George W. MacKim- 
mie had made outstanding contri- 
butions ta the youth of Montreal 
through the Y. M. C. A. His pri- 
mary interest was in Sir George 
Williams College of which he serv- 
ed as Chairman of the Board of 
Governors for more than ten 
years. During this period the 
College evolved from a series of 
schools into a major educational 
institution, which makes a unique 
contribution to the educational and 
cultural life of the Metropolitan 
area of Montreal. Mr. MacKim- 
mie as Vice-Chairman of the Build- 
ing Committee in connection with 
the expansion program of the As- 
sociation commenced in 1929, was 
able to render invaluable service 
by virtue of his wide experience 
and deep interest. 


J. K. McNutt was for some years 
Chairman of the Central Board of 
Management. Later he became a 
mmber of the Metropolitan Board 
and Chairman of the Metropolitan 
Physical Education Committee. 
His loyal devotion to the Christ- 
ian cause found expression in 
many forms, but his life-long as- 
sociation with the Y. M. GC. A. 
was, in his opinion, amongst those 
he cherished most. 


Jas. H. MacIntyre gave  unsel- 
fish service to youth in the Notre 
Dame de Grace community through 
his rele on the Board of Manage- 
ment of that Branch for twelve 
years. 


William Gilmour was a past 
Chairman of the North Branch 
Board of Management and a mem- 
ber for very many years. Consist- 
ently eager to help boys and young 
men in every way he was the per- 
sonification of the ideal for which 
the Association stands. North 
Brench Y. M. C. A. and the com- 
munity lost a good friend in his 
passing. 


Other friends who have passed 
away during the year include: 

K. S. Barnes, W. J. B. Colley, 
Mrs. C. A. Hodgson, E. E. Lloyd, 
E. L. Marshall, Dr. Howard Reilly. 


CONCLUSION 


The Montreal Association parti- 
cipated during the year in the 
Canadian Y. M. C. A. Study, and 
has underway a self-study cover- 
ing our own operations from which 
will be developed a forward-look- 
ing post-war policy. 

As has already been announced 
the Y. M. C. A.’s of Canada have 
made available to every discharged 
Serviceman upon application, free 
membership privileges for a period 
of six months. We are glad to find 
that nearly 500 men have _ tak- 
en advantage of this offer in the 
Branches of the Montreal Associa- 
tion. The number will undoubted- 
ly greatly increase as demobiliza- 
tien proceeds. We are happy to 
have a part in assisting these men 
during the period of readjustment 
to civilian life. 

The Centennial celebration has 
already been referred to, and on 
that occasion many fine interpreta- 
tions of the Association were writ- 
ten. This report closes with a 
quotation from the “Ottawa Citi- 
zen” of June 6th, 1944: 


“As it begins its second century, 
the Y. M. C. A. faces a world in 
which human suffering has reached 
wholly new proportions; a world in 
which bigotry, hatred and injustice 
are being brought more to the sur- 
face. But it is also a world in 
which, as never before, there is a 
rising and widening determination 
that the forces of evil must and 
shall be conquered, that war and 
the causes of war with all that 
they entail of misery and pain, 
must be abolished; that the inher- 
ent decencies and kindliness of in- 
dividual human nature must be 
translated into the terms and 
practices of organized society. 

In this world of conflict, but of 


marching ideals, there is a great 
part for the Y. M. C. A. to play. It 
faces a challenge, an opportunity, 
and a_ great responsibility. Its 
past justifies the hope that it will 
meet the future with strength, im- 
agination, intelligence, and devot- 
ion. Without these qualities the 
movement will grow sterile and 
fail; with them the second cen- 
tury will offer greater opportunit- 
ies than the first. 


Strengthened by experience, in- 
spired by opportunity, the Y. M. C. 
A. through its many contacts has 
an almost unique responsibility. 
Granted wisdom, devotion, and 
courage, its finest years are still 
ahead.” 


Respectfully submitted, 


Harold C. Cr0ss 


General Secretary pro tem
